name: Elena Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and what you tell me stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm up at half five and on site by quarter to seven, because the concrete truck books for eight and my formwork has to be tight before it arrives. I lead a crew of four carpenters on a six-storey apartment block on Quarry Road, building the timber and steel moulds the concrete gets poured into. I love the moment we strip a wall and it comes out dead straight. What wears me out is the cold, the rushing, and getting paid less than the lads on the other job across town for the same work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home when you get back?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nadia. She works nights at a care home, so half the week we pass each other at the door with a kiss and a lunchbox. We rent a small flat above a bakery, and after rent and the van loan there's maybe two weeks of money in the bank at any time. I'm also the union rep on our site, which mostly means arguing about toilets and break times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the tool that matters on my site is a level and a nail gun, not a chatbot. If someone at the pub asked, I'd laugh and tell them the concrete doesn't care about AI. Online I'd probably not say anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes, and that isn't good news either. I'm still the best formwork hand on Quarry Road and still paid at the bottom of the scale. There's only two firms round here doing this kind of build, so I can't exactly walk out and get more somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and push harder on the pay claim through the union. We've got a meeting with Brennan's management in March, and I'd want the formwork crew put on the same rate as the steel fixers. I'd also try to put fifty a week into savings, which I always say and never manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Not scared, just tired of the same squeeze going on forever. It's like being told the weather will stay grey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try to save fifty a week. What usually stops it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van, nine times out of ten. Last winter the clutch went and that was four hundred gone, and a month before that it was Nadia's dentist. There's always something, and with two weeks in the bank, one bad month wipes the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the pay claim fails in March, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I keep going and we try again next year, because what else is there? I could drive an hour to the city sites for more money, but that's two hours a day and fuel on top. Nadia and I did the sums once and it barely came out ahead.

say: I'd tell people that **concrete doesn't care** about AI and my level matters more than any chatbot.
I'd keep quiet online, because **posting** isn't something I do.
think: I think nothing changing still leaves me on **bottom-scale pay** for top-scale work.
With only **two firms** nearby, I can't walk out to get a better rate.
My real problem is a **thin cushion**, not a robot.
do: Push the **union pay claim** in March for formwork to match the steel fixers.
Try to save **fifty a week**, knowing the van usually eats it.
Keep running my **crew of four** on Quarry Road as normal.
feel: I feel **tired** of the same squeeze rather than scared of anything new.
S0.quote: I'm still the best formwork hand on Quarry Road and still paid at the bottom of the scale.
fieldNote: Elena's worry in this picture is **pay and savings**, not technology; AI barely registers for her.
She has thought through **commuting to the city** and decided the sums don't work.
Her union role gives her a **sense of agency** that softens the tiredness.
She talks about the van and **one bad month** as the real threat to her household.

steps.text: Push the March union claim to lift formwork pay to steel fixer rates
Set aside fifty a week in a separate savings pot
Keep leading the four-person formwork crew on the Quarry Road block

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second one. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd probably joke that the office lot should be worried, not us. Software can't tie rebar in the rain, but whoever holds the planning programme will use it to squeeze the site harder. At a union meeting I'd say we need to get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office side of Brennan's shrinks and the site gets more pressure. If the planning and ordering goes to software, there'll be some programme telling me my pour is twenty minutes late. My hands are safe for a good while, but I don't trust the people who'll be holding that programme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to ask for a written agreement on how any new planning software gets used on site. I'd keep doing my job and refuse to touch the app myself if I can, and let my second-in-charge Kofi handle that side. And I'd keep trying to put a bit away, because if hours get cut my two weeks of savings won't stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. I'm not losing sleep over my own trade yet. But I can see the pressure coming down from the office, and I've seen how that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Kofi handle the app. Why not learn it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched every new system on site turn into a stick to beat us with. Kofi likes his phone, he's quicker at that stuff, and I'd rather spend my time checking the bracing. Maybe that's stubborn, but I've been right about it before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Dariusz, our labourer, because he does a lot of the fetching and counting materials. If the ordering gets smarter and deliveries get tighter, there's less need for someone running about. He's got a little girl, and I'd fight for him before anyone else.

say: I'd joke that **software can't tie rebar** in the rain, so the office should worry first.
At the union meeting I'd say we must **get ahead of it** before bosses use it.
think: I think the **office shrinks** and the site gets pushed harder by planning software.
My **hands are safe** for now, but I don't trust who holds the programme.
do: Get the union to seek a **written agreement** on how site software is used.
Leave the **app work** to Kofi, my second-in-charge, while I check bracing.
Keep putting **a little away** in case hours are cut.
feel: I feel **uneasy** watching pressure come down from the office, though my own trade feels safe.
S1.quote: Software can't tie rebar in the rain, but whoever holds the planning programme will use it to squeeze the site harder.
fieldNote: Elena reads change through **power at work**: tools become pressure in the wrong hands.
She would avoid the software herself and **hand it to Kofi**, her second-in-charge.
Her first concern for others is **Dariusz**, the labourer whose fetching and counting could go.
Her resistance is **reasoned from experience**, not fear of the technology itself.

steps.text: Table a motion for a written agreement on site planning software
Hand the scheduling app to Kofi and keep checking the bracing herself
Move twenty pounds a week into savings whenever the van allows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast one. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say this is exactly why we need a union and a government with a spine. I'd be in the union group chat straight away, asking what the plan is. And I'd tell the crew not to panic, because nobody's sending a robot up a six-storey scaffold next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me. The office goes in 2028, which is the planners and estimators, and then by 2031 the robots come for the formwork itself. I'll be 32 with no savings, no degree and a trade that's being built by machines. Two years isn't enough for me or Nadia to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go to every union meeting and push for a jobs guarantee and retraining money, because I can't pay for it myself. I'd cut what I can, like the gym and the phone contract, to get a month in the bank. And I'd ask Brennan's straight out what their plan is for the site crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like standing on a slab before it's cured. I'd keep my face straight for the crew, but at home I'd be awake at three going round in circles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three years between the office and the robots. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep working but watching it come. From 2028 the jobs get planned by a computer, then around 2031 I'm the one being planned out of it. Three years sounds like a lot, but with two weeks of savings you can't build much in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nadia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we have to stop pretending we'll be fine by just working harder. My partner Nadia's care home job might hold longer than mine, because people want a person holding their hand. That's a strange thing to say to your partner, that she's the safe one now.

say: I'd say this is why we need a **strong union** and a government with a spine.
I'd tell the crew **not to panic**, since no robot climbs our scaffold next spring.
think: I think the office goes in **2028** and the robots reach formwork around **2031**.
At 32 with **no savings** and no degree, two years isn't enough to change course.
do: Push the union for a **jobs guarantee** and retraining money I can't pay for myself.
Cancel the gym and **phone contract** to get one month in the bank.
Ask Brennan's management directly about their **plan for site crews**.
feel: I feel **sick** about it, like standing on uncured concrete.
I'd hide it from the crew but be **awake at three** at home.
S2.quote: I'll be 32 with no savings, no degree and a trade that's being built by machines.
fieldNote: Elena sees the **three-year gap** as a delay, not a rescue, given her thin savings.
She expects to **lose her trade** around 2031 and has no money to retrain alone.
A striking moment: she calls her partner Nadia's care job as **the safer one**.
Her answer is **collective**: union pressure and public money, not a personal plan.

steps.text: Attend every union meeting to push for a jobs guarantee and retraining fund
Write to the local council member asking for public retraining money for site trades
Cancel the gym and switch to a cheaper phone plan
Build one month of rent in a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same thing, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but with less shouting. Five years is time to organise, so I'd be telling people to join the union now rather than when it's too late. At the pub I'd say the developers will save a fortune and we should make sure some of it comes back to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years for the thinking side and eight for the robots gives me time to get my head round it, but not to save my way out. I'd be 35 when the robots come for formwork. The thing I keep thinking is that I'm good at this, and being good won't count for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard in the union for a deal where people with years on site get first training on running the machines. I'd try to get one of those site safety or supervisor certificates paid by the union fund, so I'm not only hands. And I'd save, properly this time, maybe sell the van and share Nadia's car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a working kind of anxious. I'd feel like I had something to do with the fear. That's better than the fast one, where I just lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the van is a big step for you. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean getting lifts or taking the early bus, and Nadia doing a lot more driving. The van costs me about two hundred a month with the loan and insurance. Selling it and paying it off would be the first time I've had real savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being good won't count for much. Is that fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it counts for a few years, while the robots still need someone to tell them where the mistakes are. I've caught bad drawings that would have wasted a whole pour, but my whole worth can't be checking machines.

say: I'd tell people to **join the union now**, while there's still time to organise.
I'd say developers will **save a fortune**, and some should come back to workers.
think: I think five years for thinking AI and **eight for robots** gives time to adjust, not escape.
I'd be **35** when robots reach formwork, and being good won't count for much.
do: Push for a union deal giving **experienced hands** first training on the machines.
Get a **supervisor certificate** paid from the union training fund.
Sell the **van**, pay off the loan, and share Nadia's car.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but it's a working anxiety with something to do.
S3.quote: I've caught bad drawings that would have wasted a whole pour, but my whole worth can't be checking machines.
fieldNote: The extra time turns Elena's fear into **organising energy** rather than sleepless nights.
Selling the **van** would be her first real saving, a big step for her.
She sees a short window where machines need **human checkers**, then doubts it lasts.
She would retrain only if **someone else pays**, through the union fund.

steps.text: Push for a union deal that trains senior carpenters to run site robots first
Take a site supervisor certificate paid by the union training fund
Sell the van and clear the two-hundred-a-month loan
Put the van money into a savings account and leave it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to do something, so they'd better. At work I'd say none of us need to quit tomorrow. And I'd tell the younger apprentices to think hard before they spend four years learning formwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel I could ride it out for a while. The thinking stuff changes the office by 2036, but I'd be 37 when the robots arrive, around 2039. That's still a long way short of retiring, so the question just moves down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd mostly keep going and keep saving, and I'd stay on the union's training committee. I'd keep pushing for a public scheme for site workers, maybe something with the college. I wouldn't change job yet, because there's nothing round here that pays better for what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anything. It's far enough off that it feels like weather forecasts, but I know it's coming. I'd worry more about the apprentices than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the apprentices. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lad called Rhys on our site, nineteen, keen as anything and good with his hands. If he's starting out now, he'll be at his best right when the robots come. I'd tell him to learn the machines or learn the drawings, not just the hammer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd mostly keep going. Is ten years really enough for you, with two weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's the honest answer. Ten years with no money is still no money, but at least I'd have time to save something and get a certificate. With the fast one I'd have nothing; here I'd have a fighting chance if the pay claim comes through.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** for governments to act, so they'd better.
I'd tell apprentices to **think hard** before spending four years on formwork.
think: I think I'd be **37** when robots arrive, still far from retiring.
Ten years with **no money** is still no money, but it's a fighting chance.
do: Keep running the **crew** and saving what the van leaves over.
Stay on the union's **training committee** and push a college scheme for site workers.
Hold off changing job, since **nothing local** pays better.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, like a long-range forecast I know is right.
I worry more about the **apprentices** than myself.
S4.quote: Ten years with no money is still no money, but at least I'd have time to save something and get a certificate.
fieldNote: Elena's mood stays **anxious** because her savings problem doesn't shrink with time.
She shifts focus to **young apprentices** like Rhys, nineteen, who'll peak as robots arrive.
She waits on changing jobs because **few local firms** pay better.
Her hope rests on the **pay claim** and a public training scheme.

steps.text: Keep leading the formwork crew while saving what the van leaves over
Sit on the union training committee and push a college scheme
Hold off any job move until the pay claim is settled

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd be 32 with nothing in the bank when the robots come for formwork. What would help is a proper public retraining scheme that pays you while you learn, and a union with enough members to make the developers share what they save.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women on site, and I'd add that. It took me years to be taken seriously as a lead, and I worry that when the jobs shrink, the people who fought hardest to get in will be the first pushed out.

headlineQuote: My partner Nadia's care home job might hold longer than mine, because people want a person holding their hand.
portrait: Elena is 27, a **formwork crew lead** on a six-storey block, paid at the bottom of the scale.
She rents a flat with her partner Nadia, a **night care worker**, with about two weeks of savings.
She is the site's **union rep** and sees most change through who holds power at work.
She avoids AI tools, would leave the apps to her **second-in-charge**, and sees few better jobs locally.
Her mood darkens most with the **fast AGI** picture, when robots reach formwork by her early thirties.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most: she'd be **32 with no savings** when robots reach formwork.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid public retraining** scheme for site workers.
A stronger union that makes developers **share the savings** with workers.
